title: The chart showing UK pensions at the bottom of Europe compares completely different things
dek: The viral chart showing ‘UK pensions rock-bottom in Europe’ bundles incomparable figures from different countries; broken down, UK retiree income replacement ratios and poverty rates are actually respectable—the difference is whether retirement security comes from the state or from private pensions.
why: This episode dismantles a viral pension rankings chart and clarifies whether GDP should be calculated by market exchange rate or purchasing power parity—perfect for those accustomed to ‘international ranking charts’ but who have never scrutinized methodology.
who: Readers and policy observers concerned with pension policy debates, those frequently encountering ‘international ranking chart’ content, and those seeking to understand GDP methodology differences.
skip: The Loch Ness capacity discussion is purely tangential entertainment and doesn't affect the data arguments above—you can skip it.

points.h: Three incompatible measurement methods were conflated in the viral chart
points.body: The viral European pension comparison chart showed the UK at the bottom with £1,045. IFS researcher Heidi Kajalainen exposed the problem: some countries' figures were average pensions for all retirees, others were minimum guarantees for single people, while the UK's figure was ‘those receiving the full new state pension’—three completely different methodologies bundled into one table. Worse, Italy converted euros to pounds without adjustment, and Austria pays pensions 14 times yearly rather than 12 but didn't annualize, making one figure artificially high and the other artificially low.

points.h: UK's low state pension is supplemented by occupational pension savings
points.body: Kajalainen explained that Britain and France have completely different retirement security structures: France relies almost entirely on state pensions with minimal employer-provided occupational pensions, while Britain is the opposite—the state pension covers less than half of retirement income, the rest filled by workplace private pension savings. According to OECD 2022 data, UK retirees' average income is 84% of working-age disposable income, France's is 94%, but countries with structures closer to Britain's—the Netherlands and Denmark—are 80% and 80%, Ireland 90%—the UK performs respectably within its peer group.

points.h: French-style high pensions require French-style high taxes
points.body: If Britain wanted to emulate France by having the state pension cover more retirement income, it would need to confront the fact that France's working population pays much higher taxes and social contributions—this is a trade-off, not a one-way increase in generosity. By the latest 2024-25 data, the UK's retiree poverty rate is 14%, while the working-age poverty rate is 19% and child poverty 27%—retirees are actually the least disadvantaged of the three groups.

points.h: UK economy is vastly larger than Russia's by market exchange rates
points.body: Rees-Mogg and Tucker Carlson clashed on a show over Russia's economic size, then economist Duncan Weldon clarified with IMF data: by market exchange rates, UK GDP is roughly $4.3 trillion and Russia's $2.7 trillion—clearly Britain is larger; but using purchasing power parity (PPP), the UK becomes $4.7 trillion while Russia reaches $7.5 trillion—which method is ‘correct’ doesn't depend on politics but on what you're measuring.

points.h: Military purchasing power depends on which GDP measure you choose
points.body: Weldon noted that the two GDP measures aren't either-or—it depends on where the money is spent. If Russia is paying soldiers' salaries and domestic expenses, PPP better reflects actual purchasing power because Russia's labour costs are lower; but if importing drones and ammunition from China, it pays world market prices in hard currency, where PPP adjustment is irrelevant and unadjusted market-rate GDP determines actual military procurement capacity.

points.h: This summer's heat waves caused roughly 5,000 excess deaths
points.body: Actuary Stuart MacDonald analysed England and Wales death data and found that during five distinct heat waves this summer, about 55,000 people died, roughly 5,000 more than the expected 50,000—about 10% excess. The late June to early July heat wave caused the most harm; unlike the May heat wave (which showed the ‘harvesting effect’ of brought-forward deaths), the June and August heat waves showed no subsequent mortality dip, resembling instead the continental European pattern of genuinely increasing total deaths.

points.h: But 2026 overall had substantially lower death rates than last year
points.body: Looking at the full year reverses the picture entirely: 2026 death rates so far are about 2% lower than last year, equivalent to roughly 8,500 fewer deaths if 2025 rates had continued. One major reason is flu deaths plummeting—roughly 50,000 so far this year, far below last year's 58,000 and 2024's 60,000—contradicting last winter's NHS England warning of a ‘super-flu’.

points.h: Loch Ness could theoretically hold Earth's entire population
points.body: Using the standard physics approximation of 100 litres per human body, and Loch Ness's capacity of roughly 745.2 billion litres, that yields roughly 10 times Earth's current population; considering 100 litres is deliberately overestimated and real volume is probably 60-70 litres, expert Keith Still thinks fitting 14 times the world population is mathematically sound—assuming you liquefy everyone first. If instead you pack people standing in a virtual multi-level car park structure, Loch Ness's average 123-metre depth could theoretically hold roughly twice the world population.

quotes.text: Well, I think they get a raw deal, to be honest. Pensioners are getting £12,500. It's not hundreds of thousands of pounds that they're getting. We pay less state pension than Ireland, for goodness sake. We're the sixth richest economy in the world.
it is true that the UK state pension is lower than public pensions that are paid in many other countries. But it is really misleading to just look at that number.
what we see is that the UK economy is worth something like $4.3 trillion, and Russia's economy is worth something like $2.7 trillion.
Now, using the International Monetary Fund's numbers on PPP size of economies, we get a UK economy which is worth $4.7 trillion and a Russian economy which in PPP terms is worth $7.5 trillion.

If we add up the periods around the main summer heat waves, I'd estimate that there were around 55,000 deaths across five clear heat wave periods, compared to around 50,000 that I would have expected.
